turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: This is something I thought about a lot and I've been talking to a lot of experts in AI security recently, and I'm something of an expert in attacking, but wouldn't really call myself an expert in defending, especially not at a model level. But I'm happy to criticize. And so in my professional opinion there's been no meaningful progress made towards solving adversarial robustness, prompt injection jailbreaking in the last couple of years since the problem was discovered. And we're often seeing new techniques come out, maybe there are new guardrails, types of guardrails, maybe new training paradigms, but it's not that much harder to do prompt injection jailbreaking still. That being said, if you look at Anthropic's constitutional classifiers, it's much more difficult to get CBRN information out of Claude models than it used to be, but humans can still do it in, I'd say, under an hour, and automated systems can still do it. (01:13:20): And even the way that they report their adversarial robustness still relies a lot on static evaluations where they say, "Hey, we have this data set of malicious prompts, which were usually constructed to attack a particular earlier model." And then they're like, "Hey, we're going to apply them to our new model." And it's just not a fair comparison because they weren't made for that newer model. So the way companies report their adversarial robustness is evolving and hopefully will improve to include more human evals. Anthropic is definitely doing this, OpenAI is doing this, other companies are doing this, but I think they need to focus on adaptive evaluations rather than static datasets, which are really quite useless. There's also some ideas that I've had and spoken with different experts about, which focus on training mechanisms. (01:14:24): There are theoretically ways to train the eyes to be smarter, to be more adversarially robust, and we haven't really seen this yet, but there's this idea that if you start doing adversarial training in pre-training earlier in the training stack, so when the AI is a very, very small baby, you're being adversarial towards it and training it then, then it's more robust, but I think we haven't seen the resources really deployed to do that.
turns.zh: 这是我深思熟虑过很多次的问题。最近我和很多AI安全领域的专家交流过，我在攻击方面算是个专家，但在防御方面，尤其是模型层面的防御，我不敢自诩。但我乐于提出批评。在我看来，自从发现问题以来，过去几年里，在解决对抗性鲁棒性和提示注入越狱攻击方面没有取得任何实质性进展。我们经常看到新技术出现，也许会有新的防护措施、防护机制，或许还有新的训练范式，但要实现提示注入越狱攻击仍然没那么难。话说回来，如果看看Anthropic的宪法分类器，从Claude模型中提取CBRN信息比以前难多了。但人类仍然能在不到一小时内做到，自动化系统也能做到。（01:13:20）甚至他们报告对抗性鲁棒性的方式仍然严重依赖静态评估，他们会说：“嘿，我们有这个恶意提示数据集，通常是用来攻击某个早期模型的。”然后他们会说：“嘿，我们要把它们应用到我们的新模型上。” 但这根本不是公平的比较，因为这些数据集不是为新模型设计的。所以公司报告对抗性鲁棒性的方式正在改进，希望能加入更多人工评估。Anthropic肯定在这么做，OpenAI也在做，其他公司也在做，但我认为他们需要关注适应性评估，而不是静态数据集，后者实在没什么用处。我还有一些想法，和不同专家讨论过，主要集中在训练机制上。（01:14:24）理论上有办法让模型更聪明、更具对抗性鲁棒性，但我们还没真正看到这些方法被应用。比如，如果在预训练阶段更早地对模型进行对抗性训练，当AI还是个非常非常小的婴儿时，就对它进行对抗性训练，这样它就能更鲁棒。但我觉得目前还没有看到真正为此投入资源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm imagining in there is an orphan just having a really hard life and just they grew up really tough, they have such street smarts, and they're not going to let you get away with telling you how to build a bomb. That's so funny how it's such a metaphor for humans in a way.
turns.zh: 我脑海中浮现的是一个孤儿，过着艰难的生活。他们在街头智慧成长，绝不会让你轻易告诉他们如何制造炸弹。这真是个绝妙的比喻，在某种程度上它也暗喻着人类的生存法则。

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: Yeah, it is quite interesting. Hopefully it doesn't turn the AI crazier or something like that, because that would become a really angry person.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实很有趣。希望这不会让AI变得更疯狂之类的，因为那样的话就真的很危险了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. [inaudible 01:15:31] also also be quite bad.
turns.zh: 是的。[1:15:31未听清]也会很糟糕。

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: So that seems to be a potential direction, maybe a promising direction. I think another thing worth pointing out is looking at anthropic constitutional classifiers and other models, it does seem to be more difficult to elicit CBRN and other really harmful outputs from chatbots, but solving indirect prompt injection, which is basically prompt injection against agents done by external people on the internet is still very, very, very unsolved, and it's much more difficult to solve this problem than it is to stop CBRN elicitation, because with that kind of information, as one of my advisors just noted, it's easier to tell the model, "Never do this," than with emails and stuff, "Sometimes do this." So with CBRN instead you can be like, "Never, ever talk about how to build a bomb, how to build atomic weapon. Never." But with sending an email, you have to be like, "Hey, definitely help out send emails, oh, but unless there's something weird going on, then don't send email." (01:16:55): So for those actions, it's much harder to describe and train the AI on the line, the line not to cross and how to not be tricked. So it's a much more difficult problem. And I think adversarial training deeper in this stack is somewhat promising. I think new architectures are perhaps more promising. There's also an idea that as AI capabilities improve, adversarial robustness will just improve as a result of that. And I don't think we've really seen that so far. If you look at the static benchmarking, you can see that, but if you look at it still takes humans under an hour, it's not like you need nation state resources to trick these models. Anyone can still do it. And from that perspective, we haven't made too much progress in robustifying these models.
turns.zh: 所以这似乎是一个潜在的方向，或许是一个很有前景的方向。我认为另一个值得指出的是，看看人类常识分类器和其他模型，从聊天机器人中引出CBRN（化学、生物、放射性武器）及其他真正危险的输出似乎更困难，但解决间接提示注入问题——即外部人员通过互联网对智能体进行的提示注入——仍然非常、非常、非常棘手。这比阻止CBRN引出更难解决，因为正如我的一位导师所指出的，对于这类信息，告诉模型“永远不要这样做”比对邮件之类的“有时可以这样做”要容易得多。对于CBRN，你可以说“永远、永远不要谈论如何制造炸弹、如何制造原子武器。永远不要。”但对于发送邮件，你必须说“嘿，一定要帮忙发邮件，哦，但除非有什么异常情况，否则不要发邮件。”（1:16:55）所以对于这些行为，要描述并训练AI不越界、不被欺骗要困难得多。这是一个更难解决的问题。我认为在这一领域进行更深入的对抗性训练还是有希望的。我认为新架构可能更有前景。还有一种观点，随着AI能力的提高，对抗性鲁棒性也会随之提高。但我认为到目前为止我们还没有真正看到这一点。如果你看静态基准测试，你可以看到这一点，但如果你看看人类仍然需要不到一个小时的时间来做到这一点，那就不是需要国家级资源才能欺骗这些模型了。任何人都可以做到。从这个角度来看，我们在增强这些模型的鲁棒性方面还没有取得太大进展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, I think what's really interesting is your point that Anthropic and Claude are the best at this, I think that alone is really interesting that there's progress to be made. Is there anyone else that's doing this well that you want to shout out just like, "Okay, there's good stuff happening here," either a company, AI company or other models?
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为真正有趣的是你提到Anthropic和Claude在这方面做得最好，我认为仅此一点就很有趣，说明确实有进步空间。还有其他在这方面做得很好的公司或模型，你想特别提一下吗？比如，“好吧，这里正在发生一些不错的事情。”

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: I think the teams at the frontier Labs that are working on security are doing the best they can. I'd like to see more resources devoted to this because I think that it's a problem that just will require more resources. I guess from that perspective I'm shouting out most of the frontier labs, but if we want to talk about maybe companies that seem to be doing a good job in AI security that are not labs, there's a couple I've been thinking about recently. And so one of the spaces that I think is really valuable to be working in is governance and compliance. There's all these different AI legislations coming out and somebody's got to help you keep track, keep up to date on all that stuff. And so one company that I know has been doing this, actually, I know the founder, I spoke to him some time ago, is a company called Trustible, with an I near the end, and they basically do compliance and governance. (01:19:23): And I remember talking to him a long time ago, maybe even before ChatGPT came out, and he was telling me about this stuff. And I was like, "Ah, I don't know how much legislation there's going to be. I don't know." But there's quite a bit of legislation coming out about AI, how to use it, how you can use it, and there's only going to be more and it's only going to get more complicated. So I think companies like Trustible and how them in particular are doing really good work. And I guess maybe they're not technically an AI security company, I'm not sure how to classify them exactly, but, anyways, if you want a company that is more, I guess technically AI security, Repello is when I saw that at first they seemed to be doing just automated red teaming and guardrails, which I was not particularly pleased to see, and they still do for that matter, but recently I've been seeing them put out some products that I think are just super useful. (01:20:31): And one of them was a product that looked at a company's systems and figures out what AIs are even running at the company. And the idea is they go and talk to the CISO and the CISO would be like... Or they'd say to the CISO, "Oh, how much AI deployment do you have? What do you got running?" And the CEO's like, "Oh, we have three chatbots." And then Repello would run their system on the company's internals and be like, "Hey, you actually have 16 chatbots and five other AI systems." Like, "Did you know that? Were you aware of that?" And that might just be a failure in the company's governance and internal work, but I thought that was really interesting and pretty valuable, because I've even seen AI systems we deployed that just forgot about and then it's like, "Oh, that is still running. We're still burning credits on. Why?" And I think they both deserve a shout-out.
turns.zh: 我认为前沿实验室中致力于安全领域的团队已经尽了最大努力。但我希望能投入更多资源来解决这个问题，因为这确实需要更多资源。从这个角度来看，我要为大多数前沿实验室点赞。不过，如果我们要谈论那些在AI安全方面表现出色的非实验室公司，最近我也一直在关注几家公司。其中，我认为治理与合规领域的工作非常有价值。各国正在出台越来越多的AI相关立法，有人需要帮助企业跟上这些动态。例如，我认识一家名为Trustible（Trustible，Trustible）的公司，创始人我曾与他交谈过。他们专注于合规与治理工作。（01:19:23）我记得很久以前与他交流过，可能是在ChatGPT问世之前，他就向我介绍了相关内容。我当时心想：“天啊，我不知道会有多少相关立法啊。”但关于AI的立法确实层出不穷，规范其应用的条款也越来越多，且未来只会变得更加复杂。因此，我认为像Trustible这样的公司做得非常出色。虽说严格来说它不算AI安全公司，但我不确定该如何给它归类。不过，如果你想找一家更纯粹的AI安全公司，那Repello可能更合适。我最初看到他们主要做自动化红队测试和安全防护措施时不太感冒，不过最近他们的产品让我眼前一亮。（01:20:31）其中一款产品能扫描公司系统，识别正在运行的AI模型。具体流程是，他们会与首席信息安全官沟通，询问：“你们部署了多少AI系统？都在用什么？” 首席执行官可能会回答：“我们有三个聊天机器人。”而Repello通过内部扫描发现公司实际运行着16个聊天机器人和其他5个AI系统。这类发现可能暴露出公司治理和内部管控的漏洞，但我认为这项技术非常实用。我甚至见过我们部署的AI系统被遗忘后仍在运行的情况，追问之下才发现“天啊，这个系统还在运转，我们还在消耗资源？为什么呢？” 这两家公司都值得称赞。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The last one is interesting, it connects to your advice, which is education and understanding information are a big chunk of the solution. It's not some plug and play solution that will solve your problems.
turns.zh: 最后一段很有意思，它与你的建议相呼应，即教育和信息理解是解决方案的重要组成部分。这不是一个可以直接套用就能解决问题的方案。

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Maybe a final question. So at this point, hopefully this conversation raises people's awareness and fear levels and understanding of what could happen. So far nothing crazy has happened. I imagine as things start to break and this becomes a bigger problem, it'll become a bigger priority for people. If you had to just predict, say, over the next six months, year, couple years, how you think things will play out, what would be your prediction?
turns.zh: 好的。或许最后一个问题。到目前为止，希望这次对话能提高人们的警惕性、增强他们的担忧，并让他们更清楚可能发生的情况。到目前为止，还没有出现什么特别严重的情况。我想，随着事情开始恶化，这将成为人们更优先关注的问题。如果你必须预测一下未来六个月、一年、两年内的情况，你认为会如何发展？

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: When it comes to AI security, the AI security industry in particular, I think we're going to see a market correction in the next year, maybe in the next six months, where companies realize that these guardrails don't work. And we've seen a ton of big acquisitions on these companies where it's a classical cybersecurity companies like, "Hey, we got to get into the AI stuff," and they buy an AI security company for a lot of money. And I actually don't think these AI security companies, these guardrail companies are doing much revenue. I know that, in fact, from speaking to some of these folks. And I think the idea is like, "Hey, we got some initial revenue, look at what we're going to do." (01:23:18): But I don't really see that playing out. And I don't know companies who are like, "Oh yeah, we're definitely buying AI guardrails. That's a top priority for us." And I guess part of it, maybe it's difficult to prioritize security or it's difficult to measure the results, and also companies are not deploying agentic systems that can be damaging that often, and that's the only time where you would really care about security. So I think there's going to be a big market correction in there where the revenue just completely dries up for these guardrails and automated red teaming companies. Oh, and the other thing to notice, there's just tons of these solutions out there for free, open source, and many of these solutions are better than the ones that are being deployed by the companies. So I think we'll see a market reaction there. I don't think we're going to see any significant progress in solving adversarial robustness in the next year. (01:24:23): Again, this is something it's not a new problem, it's been around for many years, and there has not been all that much progress in solving it for many years. And I think very interestingly here, with image classifiers, there's a whole big ML robustness, adversarial robustness around image classifiers, people are like, "What if it classifies that stop sign as not a stop sign and stuff like that?" And it just never really ended up being a problem. Nobody went through the effort of placing tape on the stop sign in the exact way to trick the self-driving car into thinking it's not a stop sign. But what we're starting to see with LLM powered agents is that they can be tricked and we can immediately see the consequences, and there will be consequences. And so we're finally in a situation where the systems are powerful enough to cause real world harms. And I think we'll start to see those real world harms in the next year.
turns.zh: 谈到人工智能安全，尤其是人工智能安全行业，我认为未来一年内可能会出现市场调整，可能是未来六个月内。公司会意识到这些防护措施并不奏效。我们看到很多大公司收购其他公司，特别是传统网络安全公司，比如“嘿，我们得进军人工智能领域”，然后花大价钱收购人工智能安全公司。但我认为这些人工智能安全公司、防护措施公司并没有创造太多收入。事实上，我和一些业内人士交流过，他们承认这一点。他们可能只是想：“我们刚获得了初始收入，看看接下来要做什么。”（01:23:18）但我觉得这种情况不会持续下去。我没听说过有哪家公司会说：“哦，对，我们肯定要购买人工智能防护措施。这是我们的首要任务。” 我觉得部分原因可能是，安全问题很难优先级排序，效果也很难衡量。此外，很多公司并不常部署可能造成破坏的主动防御系统，而只有在这种情况下人们才会真正重视安全。因此，防护措施和自动化红队公司将面临市场调整，收入将彻底枯竭。哦，还有一点值得注意的是，市面上有很多免费的开源解决方案，其中许多甚至比企业部署的系统更出色。所以我认为市场会对此做出反应。我认为未来一年内在解决对抗性鲁棒性方面不会有重大进展。（01:24:23）再说一次，这不是一个新问题，多年来一直存在，但多年来进展甚微。有趣的是，在图像分类器领域，人们一直在研究图像分类器的ML鲁棒性和对抗性鲁棒性。比如，“如果它把停车标志分类成不是停车标志会怎样？”但这从未真正成为问题。没有人费心用胶带精确模拟停车标志来欺骗自动驾驶汽车认为那不是停车标志。但现在我们开始看到，基于LLM的智能体可以被欺骗，我们能立即看到后果，而且这些后果是真实存在的。所以我们终于到了一个系统强大到足以造成现实世界伤害的阶段。我认为未来一年内我们会开始看到这些现实世界的伤害。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else that you think is important for people to hear before we wrap up? I'm going to skip the lightning round. This is a serious topic. We don't need to get into a whole list of random questions. Is there anything else that we haven't touched on? Anything else you want to just double down on before we wrap up?
turns.zh: 在结束之前，你觉得还有什么对人们来说很重要的事情需要听一听吗？我就不玩闪电问答环节了。这是一个严肃的话题。我们不需要一堆随机问题。还有什么我们没有讨论到的吗？在结束之前，你还有什么想重点强调的？

turns.speaker: Sander Schulhoff
turns.en: One thing is that if you're, I don't know, maybe a researcher or trying to figure out how to attack models better, don't try to attack models, do not do offensive adversarial security research. There's an article, a blog post out there called Do not write that jailbreak paper. And basically the sentiment it and I are conveying is that we know the models can be broken, we know they can be broken in a thousand million ways. We don't need to keep knowing that. And it is fun to do AI red teaming against models and stuff, no doubt, but it's no longer a meaningful contribution to improving defensiveness. (01:26:38): And, if anything, it's just giving people attacks that they can more easily use. So that's not particularly helpful, although it's definitely fun. And it is helpful actually, I will say, to keep reminding people that this is a problem so they don't deploy these systems. So another piece of advice from one of my advisors. And then the other note I have is there's a lot of theoretical solutions or pseudo solutions to this that center around human in the loop like, "Hey, if we flag something weird, can we elevate it to a human? Can we ask a human every time there's a potentially malicious action?" And these are great from a security perspective, very good. But what we want, what people want is AIs that just go and do stuff. Just go just get it done. I don't want to hear from you until it's done. That's what people want and that's what the market and the AI companies, the frontier labs will eventually give us. (01:27:54): And so I'm concerned that research in that middle direction of like, "Oh, what if we ask the human every time there's a potential problem?" It's not that useful because that's just not how the systems will eventually work. Although I suppose it is useful right now. So I'll just share my final takeaways here. And the first one, guardrails don't work, they just don't work, they really don't work. And they're quite likely to make you overconfident in your security posture, which is a really big, big problem. And the reason I'm mentioning this now, and I'm here with Lenny now, is because stuff's about to get dangerous, and up to this point it's just been deploying guardrails on chatbots and stuff that physically cannot do damage, but we're starting to see agents deployed, we're starting to see robotics deployed that are powered by LLMs, and this can do damage. (01:28:56): This can do damage to the companies deploying them, the people using them. It can cause financial loss, eventually physically injure people. So the reason I'm here is because I think this is about to start getting serious and the industry needs to take it seriously. And the other aspect is AI security, it's a really different problem than classical security. It's also different from AI security, how it was in the past. And, again, I'm back to the you can patch a bug, but you can't patch a brain. And for this you really need somebody on your team who understands this stuff, who gets this stuff. And I lean more towards AI researcher in terms of them being able to understand the AI than classical security person or classical systems person. But really you need both, you need somebody who understands the entirety of the situation, and, again, education is such an important part of the picture here.
turns.zh: 有一件事是，如果你，比如说，可能是一名研究人员，或者正试图弄清楚如何更好地攻击模型，那就别去尝试攻击模型，别做带有攻击性的对抗性安全研究。网上有一篇文章，一篇博客文章，叫做《别写那篇越狱论文》。基本上，我们传达的观点是，我们知道这些模型是可以被攻破的，我们知道它们可以被以无数种方式攻破。我们不需要一次又一次地确认这一点。在AI模型上进行红队攻击之类的活动固然有趣，但这已不再是对提升防御能力有意义的贡献了。（01:26:38）而且，如果说有什么意义的话，那就是只会让人们更容易获得可用的攻击手段。所以这并没有什么实际帮助，尽管确实很有趣。从某种程度上说，提醒人们这是一个问题，从而阻止他们部署这些系统，这才是有益的。这是我一位导师给出的建议。然后我还有另一个观点：针对这个问题，有很多理论性的解决方案或伪解决方案，比如“嘿，如果我们发现异常情况，能否将其提交给人类？每次出现潜在恶意行为时能否询问人类？”从安全角度来看，这些想法很棒，确实不错。但人们真正想要的，是让AI能够自动完成任务。直到任务完成，我才想听你汇报。这才是人们的需求，也是市场和AI公司、前沿实验室最终会提供的。（01:27:54）所以我担心，像“每次出现潜在问题时就询问人类”这种中间派解决方案不太实用，因为这根本不符合系统最终的运作方式。不过我觉得目前这种方法还是有用的。所以我在这里分享一下我的最终看法。第一，防护措施不管用，它们就是不管用，真的不管用。而且它们很可能会让你对自己的安全防御措施过于自信，这是一个非常严重的问题。我现在提到这个问题，是因为我现在和Lenny在一起，而事情即将变得危险了。到目前为止，我们只是在聊天机器人之类的系统上部署防护措施，而这些系统根本无法造成伤害，但我们开始看到由LLM驱动的智能体和机器人被部署了，而这些可能会造成伤害。（01:28:56）这可能会对部署它们的公司和使用它们的人造成损害，导致经济损失，甚至对人造成身体伤害。所以我来这里是因为我认为这即将变得严重，行业需要认真对待它。另一个方面是AI安全，这与传统安全相比是一个完全不同的问题。它也与过去的AI安全有很大不同。再说一次，我回到了“你可以修补漏洞，但你无法修补大脑”的观点。在这方面，你真的需要团队中有人理解这些东西，有人能领会其中的门道。相较于传统安全人员或系统工程师，我更倾向于让AI研究人员来理解AI，但实际上你需要两者，你需要一个能理解整个局势的人，而教育在这方面是至关重要的。
